name: Priya Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate between Sinhala and English, mostly for families and small businesses in our community: wedding documents, shop leases, letters from the tax office. A community agency also books me to sit with older people at doctor's appointments, because many of the aunties only speak Sinhala. I work from my bedroom at my parents' house with a paper dictionary my teacher gave me. I like being useful to people I know; I don't like how little it pays and how slowly I still work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the money side look?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I give my mother a share for the house every month, and what's left is small. I have maybe two weeks of money saved. There's no other Sinhala translator in town, but there also isn't much work, and the agency pays the lowest rate on its list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because these machines never understood our language properly anyway. I'd tell people at the temple to keep coming to me rather than using their phones. I wouldn't post anything; I don't really go online for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried even in this picture, because the work is thin and it's not growing. Young people in the community use their phones for small things already, and they only come to me for official papers. If the agency cut the doctor visits, I'd have very little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and ask the temple committee to recommend me to new families. I'd also start teaching Sinhala to children on Sunday mornings, which the temple has asked me about, for a little extra. I'd ask my uncle if he needs help with the accounts at his shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, the way I always am. It's a quiet worry that sits at the dinner table with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try the translation apps to work faster?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My teacher always said a translator should carry the words in her own head. The translation apps make our language sound like a robot reading a menu. I'd rather be slow and right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say if your work dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents would say I'm welcome at home as long as I need, and they'd mean it. My father would also say I should have studied accounting. He'd be half joking.

say: Machines **never understood** our language properly anyway.
I'd tell people at the **temple** to keep coming to me, not their phones.
think: My work is **thin** and not growing, even without AI.
If the agency cut **doctor visits**, I'd have very little left.
do: Ask the **temple committee** to recommend her to new families.
Teach **Sinhala to children** on Sunday mornings for extra money.
Offer to help with **accounts** at her uncle's shop.
feel: A **quiet worry** that sits at the dinner table with her.
S0.quote: The translation apps make our language sound like a robot reading a menu. I'd rather be slow and right.
fieldNote: Her worry comes from a **small, shrinking** community market.
She relies on **family and temple** networks rather than public help.
Her refusal of AI is rooted in her **teacher's standards**.

steps.text: Ask the temple committee to recommend her to new families
Teach Sinhala to children at the temple on Sunday mornings
Help with the accounts at her uncle's grocery shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say big technology companies are taking work from ordinary people and calling it progress. I'd say families should still use someone they trust for important papers. I'd say it at the temple and to my relatives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd lose most of the small jobs in the first year. The tax letters and shop leases would go to the phone, and the agency would try phone interpreting with an app for the aunties. Only the very official documents would be left, and not many of those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the Sunday teaching seriously and ask about more classes on Saturdays too. I'd ask my uncle for regular hours at his shop, two or three days a week. I'd keep a few translation clients and wait to see what's left after a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but I wouldn't show it at home. My mother would see it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said companies are taking work. Should the government step in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't like asking the government for things. I'd rather people looked after their own, families and the temple. But I'd want the government to stop these companies pretending a machine is a translator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in the community?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The aunties at the doctor's. Mrs. Perera (an elderly neighbour) won't understand a phone talking to her about her heart. She holds my hand in the waiting room.

say: Big **technology companies** take work from ordinary people and call it progress.
Families should use someone they **trust** for important papers.
think: I'd lose **most small jobs** in the first year.
The agency would try **app interpreting** for the aunties.
do: Add **Saturday classes** to her Sunday teaching.
Ask her uncle for **regular shop hours** two or three days a week.
Keep a few clients and **wait a year** to see what's left.
feel: **Frightened**, hiding it at home though her mother sees it.
S1.quote: Mrs. Perera (an elderly neighbour) won't understand a phone talking to her about her heart.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose most** of her income quickly.
She wants companies **stopped**, not handouts for herself.
Her deepest concern is for **elderly patients** she interprets for.

steps.text: Add Saturday Sinhala classes at the temple
Ask her uncle for two or three regular days at his shop
Keep a few translation clients and review after a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a very bad thing, and people have forgotten what work is for. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen at the temple. I'd pray about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, there's no translation work left for me by 2028. I'd become someone who helps in the family shop. That's not shameful, but it's not what I studied for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work at my uncle's shop full-time, stacking shelves and serving, which lasts until robots around 2031. I'd keep teaching Sinhala to children, because parents want a person for that. And I'd stay with my parents and give my mother more for the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the thing I built my life around just disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after 2031, when robots arrive for the shop work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. My uncle can't afford a robot, I think, so maybe the shop carries on. Small family shops survive a lot of things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept government support if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it were for everyone, maybe. I wouldn't line up for a handout while I could still work in the shop. My father would feel the same.

say: This is a **very bad thing**, and people forget what work is for.
I'd speak about it at the **temple** and pray about it.
think: There's **no translation work** left for me by 2028.
I'd become the **shop helper**, which isn't shameful but isn't what I studied.
do: Work **full-time** at her uncle's shop until robots around 2031.
Keep teaching **Sinhala to children** on weekends.
Give her mother **more for the house** while living at home.
feel: **Alarmed**, as the thing she built her life around disappears.
S2.quote: Small family shops survive a lot of things.
fieldNote: Her family **shop and home** keep her from panic.
She uses the **robot gap** for shop work, hoping small shops last.
She'd refuse a **handout** while work is available.

steps.text: Work full-time at her uncle's grocery shop
Keep teaching Sinhala to children on weekends
Stay at her parents' home and give more for the house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning and people should listen to their elders and learn a practical skill. I'd tell the young ones at the temple not to rely on screens. I wouldn't say much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd lose the translation work a few years before 2031, and I'd waste some of the time hoping it doesn't happen. That's my nature. I'd only move when the work actually stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating as long as people come, and teach at the temple. I'd start working Saturdays at the shop now, so the move later is easier. I'd save whatever I can, maybe from the teaching money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, heavy. It's like watching rain clouds and knowing you left the washing out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you know you'd wait too long, what would push you to act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother would say I can't keep waiting for work that doesn't come. I listen when my mother says something twice. She'd say it directly, at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you thought about marriage or family in these plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents have started asking about marriage. I'd want to have steady work first, so I'm not a burden on a new family. In this picture, I'd probably wait.

say: Five years is a **warning**, so listen to elders and learn a practical skill.
Young people at the temple shouldn't **rely on screens**.
think: I'd **lose translation** a few years before 2031.
I'd **waste time** hoping and only move when work stopped.
do: Keep translating and **teaching** while people come.
Start **Saturday shifts** at the shop now.
Save what she can from the **teaching money**.
feel: **Worried and heavy**, like rain clouds over washing left out.
S3.quote: My mother would say I can't keep waiting for work that doesn't come. I listen when my mother says something twice.
fieldNote: She admits her **resistance** will waste time.
Her **mother** is the push that would make her act.
She'd **delay marriage** until work feels steady, so she isn't a burden on a new family.

steps.text: Start Saturday shifts at her uncle's shop
Save the money from Sunday teaching
Delay marriage plans until she has steady work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough for families to prepare properly. I'd tell people to keep their children close to the community and to useful work. I'd sound calmer than in the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still lose the translating, but slowly. I'd be thirty-seven, and that's still young enough to build something, maybe a proper teaching job or a share in the shop. I'd probably marry in that time too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating and teaching for a few years and do a teaching assistant course in the evenings around 2028. I'd save a little every month and ask my uncle about taking on part of the shop later. I'd wait before making big changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I could sleep. It feels far enough away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A share of the shop. Has your uncle mentioned that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle has no children, and he's said he'd like the shop to stay in the family. He's mentioned it once or twice. I've never taken it seriously. In this picture, I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss most about translation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weddings. Translating a couple's documents so they can marry, and then being invited to the wedding. That happened twice last year.

say: Ten years is long enough for **families to prepare**.
Keep children close to the **community** and useful work.
think: At thirty-seven I could build **teaching or the shop**, and maybe marry.
do: Do a **teaching assistant** course in the evenings around 2028.
Ask her uncle about a **share of the shop** later.
S4.quote: My uncle has no children, and he's said he'd like the shop to stay in the family.
fieldNote: With time, the **family shop** becomes a real future, not just a refuge.
Her income still ends, so her **thin savings** keep her anxious.
She misses **weddings** most, which says a lot about her values.

steps.text: Take an evening teaching assistant course around 2028
Save a small amount from every translation job
Ask her uncle about taking a share of the shop
Keep translating for community families for a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd go from translator to shop helper almost overnight. What would help is support for families and small community businesses, like my uncle's shop, so they can take on young people. Not handouts, but a way to keep working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the aunties again. When I'm not there, who will hold their hands in the waiting room? A phone can say the words, but a phone can't sit with you.

headlineQuote: A phone can say the words, but a phone can't sit with you.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old** Sinhala–English translator for her community and elderly patients at the doctor's.
She lives with her **parents**, gives her mother money for the house, and has two weeks saved.
She never uses AI, trusting her **teacher's standards** and her paper dictionary.
She blames **technology companies**, prefers family and temple support, and would refuse handouts while she can work.
Her mood stays **alarmed** in most pictures, easing to anxious with ten years and a family shop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, going from translator to shop helper almost overnight.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **small community businesses** so they can employ young people.
